dervis-irab:13-19.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْقَرْيَةِ): qarya, with fatḥa or kasra on the qāf: the estate (ḍayʿa), the great city (miṣr jāmiʿ), and the gathering of people. The plural is qurā, and the relative adjective is qarawī or qarayī. What is meant by it here is Antioch, and something about it will come in the section on benefits.
(فَعَزَّزْنا): "we strengthened".
(طائِرُكُمْ): It was mentioned earlier in this book. In al-Mukhtār: "A person's ṭāʾir is his deed, which has been hung around his neck. Al-ṭayr is also the noun from taṭayyur (omen-taking), and from it comes their saying:
There is no omen except the omen of Allah, just as it is said, there is no command except the command of Allah. Ibn al-Sikkīt said:
One says, "the omen of Allah, not your omen", and one does not say "the omen (ṭayr) of Allah". One takes an omen (taṭayyara) from a thing or by a thing, and the noun is al-ṭira, on the pattern of ʿinaba, which is what one regards as ill-omened from a bad augury." [Translator's note: the closing quotation mark of this quotation is missing in the source.]

* I'rab:
(وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلًا أَصْحابَ الْقَرْيَةِ إِذْ جاءَهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ): A resumptive clause, introduced to command the Prophet to set forth for his people a parable about the people of the town. (واضرب) is an imperative verb meaning "make"; (لهم) is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), because it was originally an adjective of (مثلا) and was put before it; (مثلا) is the second direct object of (اضرب); and (أصحاب) is the first direct object. It is useful to cite the words of Abū al-Suʿūd in his tafsīr, which are: "Setting forth a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is used sometimes for applying a strange situation to another like it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ضرب الله مثلا للذين كفروا امرأة نوح وامرأة لوط﴾ ('Allah sets forth as a parable for those who disbelieved the wife of Nūḥ and the wife of Lūṭ'), and at other times for mentioning a strange situation and explaining it to people without intending to apply it to a counterpart of it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وضربنا لكم الأمثال﴾ ('and We set forth for you the parables'). So the meaning according to the first is: make the people of the town a parable for these people in their excess in disbelief and their persistence in denying the messengers, that is, apply their situation to the situation of those; with (مثلا) as the second object of (اضرب) and (أصحاب القرية) its first object, put after it so that what explains and clarifies it may be joined to it. According to the second, it is: mention to them, and explain to them, a story which in its strangeness is like a parable." On this basis (اضرب) would mean "mention", (مثلا) would be a direct object, and (أصحاب) a badal (substitute) on the omission of a muḍāf, that is, "the parable of the people of"; but the first is preferable. (إذ) is an adverb for past time, and its position is a badal ishtimāl (inclusive substitute) from (أصحاب القرية); and the clause (جاءها المرسلون) is in the position of a genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it.
(إِذْ أَرْسَلْنا إِلَيْهِمُ اثْنَيْنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُما): (إذ) is an adverb, a substitute for the first (إذ), that is, a detailed substitute for a summarised one, which falls within the scope of the badal muṭābiq (congruent substitute) or "substitute of the whole for the whole". The clause (أرسلنا) is in the position of a genitive by annexation; (إليهم) is attached to (أرسلنا); (اثنين) is the direct object of (أرسلنا); the fāʾ is a conjunction; and (كذبوهما) is a past verb, an agent and a direct object. (فَعَزَّزْنا بِثالِثٍ فَقالُوا إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ مُرْسَلُونَ): The fāʾ is a conjunction, and (عززنا) is a past verb and an agent; (بثالث) is attached to (عززنا); (فقالوا) is conjoined to (فعززنا); then inna and its noun; (إليكم) is attached to (مرسلون); (مرسلون) is the khabar of inna, and the clause is the content of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). The direct object of (عززنا) is omitted, and the secret of its omission will come in the section on rhetoric. (قالُوا: ما أَنْتُمْ إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُنا): (قالوا) is a verb and an agent; (ما) is negative; (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (بشر) is the khabar of (أنتم); (مثلنا) is an adjective of (بشر); the address is to the three; and the clause (ما أنتم) is the content of the saying. (وَما أَنْزَلَ الرَّحْمنُ مِنْ شَيْءٍ إِنْ أَنْتُمْ إِلَّا تَكْذِبُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is negative; (أنزل الرحمن) is a verb and an agent; (من) is a redundant preposition, and (شيء) is genitive in form because of (من) but accusative in position as the direct object of (أنزل); (إن) is negative; (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; and the clause (تكذبون) is the khabar.
(قالُوا رَبُّنا يَعْلَمُ إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ لَمُرْسَلُونَ): (ربنا) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (يعلم) is the khabar, the agent of (يعلم) being a latent pronoun, its implied form being "huwa" (he); then inna and its noun, its hamza being given kasra because of the lām in its khabar; (إليكم) is attached to (مرسلون); the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (مرسلون) is the khabar of (إنا); and the clause (إنا إليكم لمرسلون) takes the place of the two objects of (يعلم). The discussion of the emphasis of the report will come in the section on rhetoric. (وَما عَلَيْنا إِلَّا الْبَلاغُ الْمُبِينُ): The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is negative; (علينا) is a fronted khabar; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (البلاغ) is a postponed mubtadaʾ; and (المبين) is an adjective. (قالُوا: إِنَّا تَطَيَّرْنا بِكُمْ): (قالوا) is a verb and an agent; then inna and its noun, its hamza being given kasra because it occurs after the verb "to say"; the clause (تطيرنا) is its khabar; and (بكم) is attached to (تطيرنا). The reason for their taking an omen was that they anticipated evil and sensed it after they had denied them, the fates of the peoples destroyed for denying the prophets having reached them.
(لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهُوا لَنَرْجُمَنَّكُمْ وَلَيَمَسَّنَّكُمْ مِنَّا عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ): In (لئن), the lām is the preparatory lām for the oath, and (إن) is conditional; (لم) is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; (تنتهوا) is an imperfect verb, jussive by (لم), and the wāw is the agent; the lām occurs in the answer to the oath; (نرجمنكم) is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on fatḥa because of its attachment to the nūn of emphasis, the heavy one («الثفيلة» in the source) [Translator's note: the source reads «الثفيلة», evidently a misprint for «الثقيلة» "the heavy"], the agent being a latent pronoun, its implied form being "naḥnu" (we), and the kāf is the direct object; and the clause has no grammatical position. The apodosis of the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to the oath, in accordance with the well-known rule. (وليمسنكم) is conjoined to (لنرجمنكم); (منا) is attached to (يمسنكم); (عذاب) is the agent; and (أليم) is its adjective. (قالُوا طائِرُكُمْ مَعَكُمْ أَإِنْ ذُكِّرْتُمْ بَلْ أَنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ مُسْرِفُونَ): (طائركم) is a mubtadaʾ; (معكم) is an adverbial attached to an omitted khabar; the hamza is for a rebuking, reproving question of denial; (إن) is conditional; (ذكرتم) is a passive past verb and is in the position of a jussive as the protasis; and the apodosis of the condition is omitted. The rule according to Sībawayh is that when a condition and a question come together, the question is answered and the apodosis of the condition is omitted, whereas others held that the condition is answered. The implied form according to Sībawayh is "tataṭayyarūn" (you take omens), and according to the others "taṭayyarū" with the jussive. (بل) is a conjunction and a particle of rejection, that is, "the matter is not so"; (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ; (قوم) is the khabar; and (مسرفون) is an adjective.

* Rhetoric:
1- Omission:
In His saying «فعززنا بثالث» there is the art of concision by omission (al-ījāz bi-l-ḥadhf). The direct object of (عززنا) has been omitted; the implied form is "fa-ʿazzaznāhumā bi-thālith" (so We strengthened the two with a third). He inclined to this omission because the purpose is concentrated on the one with whom they were strengthened, the third. When the purpose is what is intended and the speech is directed at it, everything else is cast aside. Its like is your saying "the judge ruled today by the truth": the purpose for which the sentence is delivered is your saying "by the truth", and so you leave out mention of the one ruled for and the one ruled against, and all your concern is to observe the side of the truth. The names of the three will come in the section on benefits.
2- Emphasis:
In these verses emphasis of the report appears in its finest forms. He said first «إذ أرسلنا إليهم اثنين فكذبوهما», so the speech is delivered as an initial report (ibtidāʾī al-khabar). Then he said «إنا إليكم مرسلون», emphasising it with two emphasisers, namely inna and the nominal form of the sentence, so the speech is delivered as a requested one (ṭalabī). Then he said «إنا إليكم لمرسلون», rising in emphasis to three, namely inna, the lām and the nominal form of the sentence, so the speech is delivered as a report of denial (inkārī al-khabar), as an answer to their denial. It was said that in His saying «ربنا يعلم» there is a fourth emphasis, namely making the speech take the course of an oath in emphasis, and in that it is answered with what an oath is answered with. In this verse there is also the harmony of the verse-ending with what the rest of the speech indicates, for mention of the mission prepares the way for mention of the delivery of the message (al-balāgh) and the clear statement.

* Benefits:
We mentioned in the section on vocabulary that the town is Antioch (Anṭākiya), with fatḥa or kasra on the hamza, sukūn on the nūn, kasra on the kāf and fatḥa on the lightened yāʾ. History relates, in summary: ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, sent two messengers from among the disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn) to the people of Antioch, namely Yaḥyā and Būlus, with fatḥa on the single-dotted bāʾ. When they drew near the city they saw an old man pasturing a few sheep of his, and he was Ḥabīb the carpenter. They greeted him, and the old man said to them, "Who are you two?" They said, "The messengers of ʿĪsā." He said, "Do you have a sign with you?" They said, "We heal the sick and cure the born-blind and the leper." He had a sick son, and they wiped him, and he stood up at once. Ḥabīb believed, the news spread in the city, and a great many were healed at their hands. Their talk reached the king, and he said to them, "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said, "Yes, the One who brought you and your gods into being." The people followed them and beat them, and it was also said that they were imprisoned. Then ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, sent the chief of the disciples, Shamʿūn al-Ṣafī, after them. Shamʿūn entered the city in disguise and began to associate with the king's entourage until they grew familiar with him and brought word of him to the king. The king summoned him and took to him. One day Shamʿūn said to him, "It has reached me that you imprisoned two men; have you heard what they say?" He said, "No, anger came between me and that." So he summoned them, and Shamʿūn said, "Who sent you?" They said, "Allah, who created everything and has no partner." He said, "Describe Him, and be brief." They said, "He does what He wills and rules as He wishes." He said, "And what is your sign?" They said, "Whatever the king wishes."
So he called for a boy whose eyes were blotted out, and they prayed to Allah until his sight was opened for him, and they took two pellets (bunduqatayn) and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two closed eyes with which he could see. Shamʿūn said to him, "What would you think if you asked your god to do the like of this, so that honour would be yours and his?" He said, "I have no secrets from you: our god neither sees nor hears, neither harms nor benefits." Shamʿūn used to enter with them to the idol, and he would pray and implore, and they thought he was one of them. Then he said, "If your two gods' god is able to bring a dead man back to life, we will believe in him." So they called for a boy who had died seven days before, and he stood up and said, "I was made to enter seven valleys of fire, and I warn you against what you are in, so believe." And he said, "The gates of heaven were opened and I saw a handsome young man interceding for these three." The king said, "And who are they?"
He said, "Shamʿūn and these two." The king was amazed. When Shamʿūn saw that his words had taken effect on him, he advised him and told him the situation, that he was a messenger of ʿĪsā, and called him; the king believed, and a group believed with him while others disbelieved. It was also said that rather the king disbelieved and resolved, he and his people, to kill the messengers. That reached Ḥabīb, who was at the gate of the city, and he came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the messengers.
Wahb said: Their names are Yūḥannā and Būlus; and it was said Ṣādiq and Muṣaddaq; and the third is Shamʿūn.

dervis-irab:20-29.t:
* I'rab:
(وَجاءَ مِنْ أَقْصَا الْمَدِينَةِ رَجُلٌ يَسْعى): The wāw is a conjunction or resumptive; (جاء) is a past verb; (من أقصى المدينة) is attached to (جاء); by "the city" He meant the town mentioned above, that is, Antioch; (رجل) is the agent; and the clause (يسعى) is an adjective. The man is Ḥabīb the carpenter, and a glimpse of him will come in the section on benefits. (قالَ يا قَوْمِ اتَّبِعُوا الْمُرْسَلِينَ)
(يا) is a vocative particle; (قوم) is the one addressed, a muḍāf to the omitted yāʾ of the speaker, the discussion of which has preceded; (اتبعوا) is an imperative verb and an agent; and (المرسلين) is a direct object, that is, those who are the messengers of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. (اتَّبِعُوا مَنْ لا يَسْئَلُكُمْ أَجْراً وَهُمْ مُهْتَدُونَ): (اتبعوا) is emphasis of the first; it is an imperative verb and an agent; (من) is a direct object; the clause (لا يسألكم) is its ṣila (relative clause); the kāf is the first direct object and (أجرا) the second direct object; the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl (circumstantial); (هم) is a mubtadaʾ and (مهتدون) its khabar; and the clause is accusative as a ḥāl. Some permitted that (من) be a badal from (المرسلين), and I do not know what justifies it once its governing verb is present; it is as though they imagined that an object of (اتبعوا) was omitted, and I see no need for it. More discussion of this speech will come in the section on rhetoric.
(وَما لِيَ لا أَعْبُدُ الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ; (لي) is its khabar; the clause (لا أعبد) is a ḥāl clause, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā" (I); (الذي) is its direct object; the clause (فطرني) is the ṣila; (إليه) is attached to (ترجعون); and (ترجعون) is a passive imperfect verb, the wāw being the deputy agent.
(أَأَتَّخِذُ مِنْ دُونِهِ آلِهَةً): The hamza is for a question of denial, and it is permissible that the meaning of the question be negation. (اتخذ) is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā" (I); (من دونه) is the second direct object; and (آلهة) is the first direct object. (إِنْ يُرِدْنِ الرَّحْمنُ بِضُرٍّ لا تُغْنِ عَنِّي شَفاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئاً وَلا يُنْقِذُونِ): (إن) is conditional; (يردن) is the protasis; the nūn is the protective nūn (nūn al-wiqāya), and the omitted yāʾ, omitted to follow the script of the muṣḥaf, is a direct object; (الرحمن) is the agent; (بضر) is attached to (يردن); (لا) is negative; (تغن) is the apodosis; (عني) is attached to (تغن); (شفاعتهم) is the agent; (شيئا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) or a direct object, which has often been mentioned before; (ولا ينقذون) is conjoined to (لا تغن), and the yāʾ is likewise omitted in observance of the practice of the muṣḥaf; and the conditional clause is resumptive, though it is permissible that it be an adjective of (آلهة). (إِنِّي إِذاً لَفِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ): inna and its noun; (إذن) is a particle of answer and consequence which has no effect; the lām is the shifted lām; (في ضلال) is the khabar of (إن); and (مبين) is an adjective. An important discussion of (إذن) will come in the section on benefits.
(إِنِّي آمَنْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ فَاسْمَعُونِ): inna and its noun, and the clause (آمنت) is its khabar; (بربكم) is attached to (آمنت); the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa); and (اسمعون) is an imperative verb, indeclinable by the omission of the nūn, the wāw being the agent and the omitted yāʾ a direct object. The meaning of (اسمعون) is "hear my words and follow the messengers", and in it is evidence of his firmness in his principle and the sincerity of his faith. It was also said: "hear my faith, that you may bear witness to it for me". (قِيلَ ادْخُلِ الْجَنَّةَ قالَ يا لَيْتَ قَوْمِي يَعْلَمُونَ): (قيل) is a passive past verb and what it relates to is omitted, that is, "it was said to him", at the time of his being killed and his seeing what had been prepared for him as a reward for the sincerity of his faith. (قال) is a past verb; (يا) is a particle of alerting or a vocative particle, the one addressed being omitted; (ليت) and its noun; and the clause (يعلمون) is its khabar. (بِما غَفَرَ لِي رَبِّي وَجَعَلَنِي مِنَ الْمُكْرَمِينَ): (بما) is attached to (يعلمون); (ما) is a maṣdar or a relative, that is, "of the forgiveness of my Lord" or "of that which my Lord forgave me of sins". Al-Farrāʾ said that it is interrogative, and he was answered that if it were so, its alif would have been omitted, as is the rule. It was said that omission of the alif is the more frequent practice, not a universal one; and even granting that, it is not permissible to interpret the Qur'an by the weak of the possible analyses. (جعلني) is a past verb, the nūn is the protective nūn, the yāʾ is the first direct object, and (من المكرمين) is the second direct object.
(وَما أَنْزَلْنا عَلى قَوْمِهِ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ مِنْ جُنْدٍ مِنَ السَّماءِ وَما كُنَّا مُنْزِلِينَ): A resumptive speech, delivered to show their matter to be contemptible, that is, there is no need to send armies down on them, for the least thing suffices to destroy them and uproot their hair-lock (shāʾifa). (ما) is negative; (أنزلنا) is a verb and an agent; (عليهم) is attached to (أنزلنا); (من بعده) is attached to an omitted ḥāl; (من) is a redundant preposition and (جند) is genitive in form but accusative in position as a direct object; (من السماء) is an adjective of (جند); the wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is negative; (كان) and its noun; and (منزلين) is its khabar. (إِنْ كانَتْ إِلَّا صَيْحَةً واحِدَةً فَإِذا هُمْ خامِدُونَ): (إن) is negative; (كانت) is a defective past verb whose noun is a concealed pronoun, the implied form being "mā kānat al-ṣayḥatu illā ṣayḥatan wāḥida" (it was only a single cry); the fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is the particle of surprise; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ; and (خامدون) is a khabar.

* Rhetoric:
1- The iltifāt (grammatical shift of person) in His saying «ومالي لا أعبد الذي فطرني». Its benefit is that his shift from addressing them and advising them to speaking of himself is a gentleness toward them on the one hand and a threat to them on the other. He first turned the speech to himself and showed them that he chooses for them only what he chooses for himself; then he shifted to addressing them a second time, rebuking and threatening them with the consequences awaiting them; then he returned at last to gentleness in the advice, because that is more effective in the purity of the counsel, as he wants for them only what he wants for himself. He put his saying «ومالي لا أعبد الذي فطرني» in the place of "wa-mā lakum lā taʿbudūna alladhī faṭarakum" (why do you not worship the One who created you?). Do you not see his saying «وإليه ترجعون»? Had he not intended that, he would have said "the One who created me and to whom I return". He drove it along that course until he said «إني آمنت بربكم فاسمعون». So look, O contemplative reader, at these fine points, which you pass over in the Noble Qur'an while thinking that you have understood its purport and drawn out its allusions.
2- Harmony of the verse-ending:
In His saying «قيل ادخل الجنة قال يا ليت قومي يعلمون بما غفر لي ربي وجعلني من المكرمين» there is the art of harmony of the verse-ending with what the rest of the speech indicates, for mention of Paradise prepared the way for its ending. In that is a great alert to the duty of swallowing one's rage, of forbearance toward the ignorant, and of compassion for one who has thrown himself into the throng of the wicked and the transgressors and girded himself for it. Do you not see how he wished good for those who killed him and those who lay in wait for him and watched for reverses against him and set up treacheries and ruin for him? That is one side. Then, in his wishing that they would know, there is the aim that they return to themselves after the rust is cleared from their breasts and the veils lifted from their eyes, so that dawn appears to anyone with two eyes and the darkness of doubt and falsehood is scattered. In that is victory for him and triumph (the source reads «قوز», evidently «فوز») [Translator's note: the source reads «قوز», probably a misprint for «فوز» "triumph"] for his call, and beyond that is a happiness for anyone who wants more.
3- The balīgh simile in «فإذا هم خامدون». He likened them to the extinguished fire that has become ashes, in the manner of the saying of Labīd:
وما المرء إلا كالشهاب وضوئه ... يحور رمادا إذ هو ساطع
(Man is but like a flame and its light; it turns to ashes after having shone brightly.)
That is, the state of a man, his life and his splendour, then his death and annihilation after that, is only like the state of a flame of fire and its light, which becomes ashes after its shining. After this verse:
وما المال والأهلون إلا ودائع ... ولا بدّ يوما أن ترد الودائع
(Wealth and family are but deposits, and one day the deposits must be returned.)
He likened a person's wealth and relatives to deposits, a balīgh simile, with the common ground that each of them is bound to be taken back.
4- In His saying: «قال يا قوم اتبعوا المرسلين اتبعوا من لا يسألكم أجرا وهم مهتدون»: He concluded with «وهم مهتدون» although the speech was complete without it, to add urging to follow; in it is iṭnāb (expansion).

* Benefits:
An important discussion of (إذن):
We spoke about (إذن) in this book, and we add to what has preceded what al-Raḍī said, for in it is a clarification of its place in the verse. He said: "It is a noun. Its origin is (إذ); the clause annexed to it was omitted and tanwīn was given in compensation for it, and it was given fatḥa so as to be in the form of an accusative adverb. It was intended to make it suitable for all times after it had been restricted to the past, and it was given the meaning of condition for the most part. We said 'for the most part' because there is no meaning of condition in a case like «قال فعلتها إذن وأنا من الضالين»." Then al-Raḍī said: "When it has the meaning of condition in the past, it may be made to run the course of (لو) in having its apodosis joined with the lām, as in «إذن لأذقناك» ('then We would have made you taste'), that is, 'had you inclined to them even a little, We would have made you taste'. When it has the meaning of condition in the future, its apodosis may be joined with the fāʾ, as in the saying of al-Nābigha:
ما إن أتيت بشيء أنت تكرهه ... إذن فلا رفعت سوطي إلي يدي
(I have not come with anything you dislike; if so, may my hand never raise my whip.)
that is, 'if I have come'. It may also be used after (لو) and (إن) as emphasis for the two, as in 'law zurtanī la-akramtuka' ('if you had visited me I would have honoured you') and 'in jiʾtanī idhan azūruka' ('if you come to me, then I will visit you')." Then he said: "Since (إذن), when followed by an imperfect verb, could carry the meaning of consequence, in which case the imperfect is future, and could carry the meaning of mere time, in which case the imperfect is present, and since the intention was to stipulate explicitly the meaning of consequence in (إذن), the imperfect is put in the accusative by an implied (أن), because that makes it purely future; so (إذن) is taken in its most frequent sense of consequence, since the present sense, which would prevent consequence, is excluded by the accusative caused by (أن)." Al-Raḍī went on at length in this discussion, and what we have quoted of his words suffices, to be added to what has preceded about it.

dervis-irab:30-32.t:
* I'rab:
(يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ): In this vocative there are two analyses. The first is that it is a vocative resembling a muḍāf (shibh al-muḍāf), and that is why it is accusative. It resembles a muḍāf because something that completes its meaning is attached to it, namely (على العباد). You may also make it an indefinite particularised vocative (nakira maqṣūda), as though the one addressed were a specific regret; it is accusative only because it has been described by a preposition and its genitive noun, and it has already been explained to us that an indefinite particularised vocative is accusative when it is described. The second analysis is that the one addressed is omitted and (حسرة) is a maṣdar, that is, "I lament with a lament". The commentators differed over who is lamenting, and there is no need for the difference: regret is fitting for them, and those who mock the messengers are worthy of being lamented over by the lamenters, or of lamenting over themselves. The vocative here is figurative, that is, "O regret, be present, for this is your time". (ما يَأْتِيهِمْ مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا كانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِؤُنَ): A resumptive speech, delivered to give the reason for lamenting over them. (ما) is negative; (يأتيهم) is an imperfect verb and a direct object; (من) is a redundant preposition and (رسول) is genitive in form because of (من) but nominative in position as agent; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; the clause (كانوا) is an exception from the most general of states, so it is a clause in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl from the hāʾ in (يأتيهم); (كان) and its noun; (به) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (يستهزئون); and the clause (يستهزئون) is the khabar of (كانوا).
(أَلَمْ يَرَوْا كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا قَبْلَهُمْ مِنَ الْقُرُونِ أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لا يَرْجِعُونَ): The hamza is for an affirmative question (istifhām taqrīrī), that is, "they know that well". (لم) is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; (يروا) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لم), and the wāw is the agent. (يروا) has been suspended from governing (taʿlīq), because seeing here is of the heart, i.e. knowing; (كم) is the declarative kam (khabariyya), in the position of an accusative, a fronted direct object of (أهلكنا), and the clause is in the position of an accusative as the object of (يروا); it is also permissible that (كم) be interrogative. (قبلهم) is an adverb attached to (أهلكنا); (من القرون) is a ḥāl; and (أن) and what is in its scope is a badal from the meaning of (كم أهلكنا). The implied form is: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destroying the generations before them, [and] their not returning to them?" It is also permissible that the interpreted maṣdar be the object of an omitted verb indicated by the context, the meaning being, its implied form being, "and We decreed and judged that they will not return to them". (أن) and its noun; (إليهم) is attached to (يرجعون); (لا) is negative; and the clause (يرجعون) is the khabar of (أن). Al-Zamakhsharī has a subtle discussion of it, which we cite in the section on benefits. (وَإِنْ كُلٌّ لَمَّا جَمِيعٌ لَدَيْنا مُحْضَرُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction; (إن) is negative; (كل) is a mubtadaʾ; (لما) has the meaning of (إلا); (جميع) is the khabar of (كل); (لدينا) is an adverb attached to (جميع) or to (محضرون); and (محضرون) is a second khabar. More of the i'rab of this verse and its readings will come.

* Benefits:
1- The words of al-Zamakhsharī on the verse:
The grammarians have a long discussion on the i'rab of His saying, Exalted is He: «ألم يروا كم أهلكنا قبلهم من القرون أنهم إليهم لا يرجعون». We have given you what we saw to be the best of the analyses of it, and we think it useful to give you the words that al-Zamakhsharī gave in this regard. He said: "«ألم يروا»: have they not known. It is suspended from governing in (كم), because no governor before it can govern (كم), whether it is interrogative or for a pronoun, because its origin is interrogative; but its meaning passes through the sentence, just as it passes through in your saying 'a-lam yaraw inna Zaydan la-munṭaliq' ('have they not seen that Zayd is indeed going off'), even though it does not govern its wording. «وأنهم إليهم لا يرجعون» is a badal from (كم أهلكنا) in meaning, not in wording; its implied form is: have they not seen the multitude of Our destroying the generations before them, their not returning to them."
Furthermore, (لما) has been read lightened (lammā read as lamā), in which case (إن) is the lightened form of the heavy one and is rendered inoperative; (كل) is a mubtadaʾ and what follows it is its khabar; the lām is necessarily present in the khabar to distinguish the lightened from the negative; and (ما) is redundant.
2- A subtle discussion:
Know that al-Zamakhsharī raised a question about the verse and said: How can he report about (كل) with (جميع), when al-Fārisī stated explicitly that it is not permissible to say "inna al-dhāhibata jāriyatun ṣāḥibuhā" ('the one going is the slave-girl of her owner')? They found his saying, Exalted is He, «فإن كانتا اثنتين» problematic, because it reports about the dual pronoun with the dual, so there is no benefit in it. Some people criticised al-Fārisī, saying that (الجارية) is annexed, and annexation can be on the slightest connection, so the annexation of the slave-girl to him does not indicate that she is his property; she may rather be his neighbour (jāra), and he annexed her merely in respect of neighbourliness; then he said (صاحبها), which indicated that she is his property. Al-Zamakhsharī answered the question by saying that (كل) does not require plurality (al-jamʿiyya), unlike (جميع); and Ibn ʿUṣfūr stated this explicitly, distinguishing between (أجمع) and (جميع) in that (أجمع) does not require plurality whereas (جميع) does, though he claimed that only in the accusative case, as in "jāʾa al-zaydūna jamīʿan" ('the Zayds came all together'). In the nominative there is no difference between "jāʾa al-zaydūna ajmaʿūn" and "jamīʿ". So what al-Zamakhsharī said is problematic, because (جميع) does not give plurality unless it is accusative as a ḥāl, so the question remains. Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī answered it with a good answer, namely that when the khabar contains an additional adjective or a restricting annexation, it is correct to bring the wording of the mubtadaʾ or its meaning, as in your saying "al-rajulu rajulun ṣāliḥ" ('the man is a righteous man').

dervis-irab:55-61.t:
* Vocabulary:
(شُغُلٍ): with a sukūn on the ghayn, or with a ḍamma; both were read together. In al-Qāmūs: "al-shughl with a ḍamma, with two ḍammas, with a fatḥa, or with two fatḥas, is the opposite of leisure; its plural is ashghāl and shughūl. Shaghalahu, like manaʿahu, means 'he occupied him' (shughlan, also with a ḍamma), and ashghalahu is a good, or rare, or poor usage; ishtaghala bihi and shughila, like ʿuniya, are also said, and from it one says mā ashghalahu ('how occupied he is!'), which is irregular because wonder is not expressed from a passive." The commentator on al-Qāmūs rejected ashghala and said:
It is not known to have been reported from any of the authorities of the language.
(فاكِهُونَ): enjoying ease, or delighting in bounty, from fukāha with a ḍamma, which is taking pleasure and delight, derived from al-fākiha (fruit). al-Jawharī said in his Ṣiḥāḥ:
Fukāha with a ḍamma is jesting, while fakāha with a fatḥa is the verbal noun of fakiha al-rajulu (with a kasra), so he is fakih when his life is pleasant, he is joyful and lively from luxury. So if we explain His words «فاكهون» as "enjoying ease", it is from fakāha with a fatḥa. In al-Qāmūs: "al-Fākiha is all fruit; the claim of the one who excludes dates, grapes and pomegranates from it, citing the words of the Exalted «فيهما فاكهة ونخل ورمان», is false and rejected, and I have set this out at length in al-Lāmiʿ al-Muʿlam al-ʿUjāb. Al-fākihānī is its seller; and (the form) like khajila means its eater; al-fākih is its owner; fakkahahum tafkīhan means 'he brought them fruit'; al-fākiha is also the admired palm tree, and a name for sweetmeat; fakkahahum bi-milḥ al-kalām tafkīhan means 'he amused them with it'; the noun is al-fukayha and al-fukāha with a ḍamma; fakiha, like fariḥa, fakhan and fukāhatan, so he is fakih and fākih: of good spirit, laughing, or one who talks with his companions so that he makes them laugh; from it comes taʿajjaba, like tafakkaha; and al-tafākuh is mutual jesting."
(الْأَرائِكِ): plural of arīka, which is the couch inside the ḥajala (canopied bridal chamber); it is also said to be the furnishing found in the ḥajala, (the word ḥajala being) with two fatḥas, or with a sukūn on the jīm and a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, and it is said also with a kasra on it. What is meant is something like a dome that is closed over the couch and with which the bride is adorned.
(يَدَّعُونَ): imperfect of iddaʿā, on the pattern ifʿaʿala, from daʿā yadʿū; it has been infused with the sense of wishing. Abū ʿUbayda said: "The Arabs say: idʿu ʿalayya mā shiʾta, that is, 'wish', and fulān fī khayr mā yaddaʿī, that is, 'in whatever good he wishes for'." Al-Zajjāj said: "It is from duʿāʾ (calling), that is, what they call for comes to them; and it is also said that ifʿaʿala here has the sense of tafāʿala, that is, 'what they call for among themselves'." And al-Zamakhsharī said: "yaddaʿūna is yaftaʿilūna from duʿāʾ, that is, they call for it for themselves, like your saying ishtawā and ijtamala when one roasts or melts fat for oneself. Labīd said:
وغلام أرسلته أمه ... بألوك فبذلنا ما سأل
أرسلته فأتاه رزقه ... فاشتوى ليلة ريح واجتمل
(Many a boy whose mother sent him with a message, and we gave what he asked. She sent him and his sustenance came to him, so he roasted meat for himself on a windy night and melted fat for himself.)" That is: many a boy his mother sent to us with a message, and the message here is a request, so we gave him the food he asked for right after his asking; and he made that clear by his words "she sent him and his sustenance came to him". In it is an indication that they had no food when the boy came to them, that is, his sustenance came to him from the hunt, so he roasted some of the meat for himself on a dark, windy night in which generosity is scarce, and ijtamala means he melted the fat. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "ḥamaytu al-shaḥm wa-ijtamaltuhu, when I melted it."

* I'rab:
(إِنَّ أَصْحابَ الْجَنَّةِ الْيَوْمَ فِي شُغُلٍ فاكِهُونَ): a resumptive clause, brought to affirm the condition of the people of Paradise, to enrage the disbelievers, rebuke them, and add to their regret and anguish. inna and its noun; al-yawma is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial); fī shughlin is the second khabar (predicate) of inna, and fākihūna is its first khabar, and the reverse is permissible; it is also permissible that fī shughlin be attached to fākihūna, or be in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. The meaning of shughl and fukāha will come in the section on rhetoric. (هُمْ وَأَزْواجُهُمْ فِي ظِلالٍ عَلَى الْأَرائِكِ مُتَّكِؤُنَ): hum is a mubtadaʾ (subject), azwājuhum is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to hum, and fī ẓilālin is the khabar, that is, the sun does not reach them because it is entirely absent; ʿalā al-arāʾik are two words attached to muttakiʾūna, and muttakiʾūna is a second khabar of hum; it is also permissible that His words fī ẓilālin be attached to an omitted ḥāl. (لَهُمْ فِيها فاكِهَةٌ وَلَهُمْ ما يَدَّعُونَ): lahum is a fronted khabar, fīhā are two words attached to an omitted ḥāl, fākihatun is a postponed mubtadaʾ; wa-lahum is a fronted khabar, and mā is a postponed mubtadaʾ; the clause is conjoined to the preceding clause. For mā it is permissible to be a relative noun, an indefinite qualified noun, or a maṣdar (verbal noun); and the clause yaddaʿūna has no grammatical position, or is a descriptive clause (ṣifa).
(سَلامٌ قَوْلًا مِنْ رَبٍّ رَحِيمٍ): the opinions of the grammarians differ about the i'rab of this verse, and some of them brought the discussion to six aspects. We consider it right to record the text of the statement of al-Shihāb al-Samīn for its soundness. He said: "His words salāmun: the majority read it as nominative, and there are several aspects to it. The first is that it is the khabar of mā yaddaʿūna. The second is that it is a badal (substitute) for mā, as al-Zamakhsharī said. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: If it were a substitute, then mā yaddaʿūna would be specific, whereas the apparent sense is that it is general, covering everything they call for; and if it is general, it cannot be a substitute for it.
The third is that it is an adjective of mā, and this is when you make it an indefinite qualified noun; but if you make it mean 'that which' or a maṣdar, this is impossible because of their difference in definiteness and indefiniteness. The fourth is that it is the khabar of a concealed mubtadaʾ, that is, 'it is salām'. The fifth is that it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is what governs qawlan in the accusative, that is, 'salām is said to them as a saying', and it is also said that its implied form is 'salāmun ʿalaykum'. The sixth is that it is a mubtadaʾ and its khabar is min rabbin." And qawlan is a confirmatory maṣdar for the content of the sentence, and it, together with its governing verb, is parenthetical between the mubtadaʾ and the khabar. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The most apt is that it be accusative as specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), and that is among his figurative usages." Al-Suyūṭī al-Jalāl made it accusative by removal of the preposition. Others said it is a maṣdar accusative by an omitted verb, and it, together with its governing verb, is an adjective of salām, that is, "He says to them"; and the clause salāmun qawlan min rabbin raḥīmin is in the position of accusative as the object of an omitted verb of saying; min rabbin is an adjective of qawlan, and raḥīmin is an adjective of rabbin.
(وَامْتازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ): this clause is also the object of an omitted verb of saying, that is, "and Allah says to them". wa-imtāzū is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the omission of the nūn, and the wāw is the fāʿil (agent), that is, "separate yourselves from the believers"; al-yawma is an adverb attached to imtāzū; ayyuhā is an addressed noun, indefinite but specified, from which the vocative particle has been omitted, and the hāʾ is for attention; al-mujrimūna is a badal. (أَلَمْ أَعْهَدْ إِلَيْكُمْ يا بَنِي آدَمَ): a clause arranged in the string of what is said to them, running in the manner of rebuke, reproach, silencing and constraint. The hamza is for interrogation containing these meanings; lam is a particle of negation, reversal (of tense) and jussive; aʿhad is an imperfect verb jussive by lam, its fāʿil is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā"; ilaykum is attached to aʿhad; yā is a vocative particle, banī is the one addressed, a muḍāf, and ādama is the muḍāf ilayhi.
(أَنْ لا تَعْبُدُوا الشَّيْطانَ إِنَّهُ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ): an is explicative because it occurs after a clause that has the meaning of saying without its letters; lā is prohibitive; taʿbudū is an imperfect verb jussive by the prohibitive lā, the wāw is the fāʿil, and al-shayṭāna is the direct object. It is also permissible that an be a maṣdar particle, so that it and what follows are in the position of accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "Did I not make a covenant with you to abandon the worship of Satan?" inna and its noun; lakum are two words attached to ʿaduwwun or to an omitted ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of it that was fronted; ʿaduwwun is the khabar of inna, and mubīnun is an adjective; the clause is causal for the prohibition and has no grammatical position. (وَأَنِ اعْبُدُونِي هذا صِراطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ): conjoined to an lā taʿbudū; uʿbudūnī is an imperative verb with its fāʿil and direct object; hādhā is a mubtadaʾ, ṣirāṭun is the khabar and mustaqīmun an adjective; the clause is causal for the command. The secret of placing the prohibition before the command will come in the section on rhetoric.

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain varieties of the arts of rhetoric, which we indicate in what follows:
1- The tanwīn of shughl. In it is an exaltation: that what they are occupied with is too lofty for the rank of expression to reach or for the tongue to be able to set down; and in its vagueness there is conciseness, under which is folded what cannot be counted or enumerated of the kinds of delights they enjoy in the gardens, while everything else is regarded as nothing. It also depicts what Allah has prepared for His God-fearing servants of kinds of enjoyment and varieties of pleasure: the deflowering of virgins, the hearing of strings, and visiting one another in the evenings and the early mornings. He confirmed it with the fact that they are fākihūna (enjoying ease), not occupied in mind with what occupies the minds of the people of the world, the turns of life and the preoccupations of the years, and no passing worry or descending grief spoils their serenity; and that every kind of delight to which eyes stretch and toward which imaginations travel is present with them and they obtain it while reclining on the couches, stretched out under the shade, as the description of it has been given in concrete form. All that is by way of kināya (metonymy), which has been discussed at length previously.
2- The tanwīn of ṣirāṭ. In it is magnification, as was said before, and a conciseness that points to what was covenanted to them: disobeying Satan and obeying the Most Merciful, since there is no path more upright than it. Among the examples of this tanwīn in poetry is the saying of Kuthayyir ʿAzza:
لئن كان يهدي برد أنيابها العلا ... لأفقر مني انني لفقير
(If the coolness of her upper teeth is what is being given, then he is poorer than I; indeed I am poor.)
It is also said that this verse is among the verses of al-Majnūn, and before it:
دعوت إلهي دعوة ما جهلتها ... وربي بما تخفي الصدور بصير
(I called upon my God with a call I did not misjudge, and my Lord is All-Seeing of what the breasts conceal.)
and after it:
فما أكثر الأخبار أن قد تزوجت ... فهل يأتيني بالطلاق بشير
(How abundant are the reports that she has married; will a bearer of good tidings come to me with the divorce?)
His words "لئن كان يهدي" explain the supplication that he made deliberately and with presence of heart, and what lies between them is a parenthesis for emphasis and to convey that the supplication was in secret. That is: if the coolness of her upper teeth is what is given (and he singled them out because they are the first thing to appear in smiling), then he is needier than I; I am extremely poor, worthy of being described by it because of the perfection of its conditions in me. It is also possible that "the coolness of her fangs" is a kināya for her whole self, and "indeed I am poor" is an emphasized statement indicating intensity of need and greatness of want; and what want is harder on the lover than his need for the one he loves to cure his ailments? And the an in "أن قد تزوجت" is the lightened form of the heavy (anna), and its noun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn); it is on the assumption of a preposition, that is: "I wonder at the multitude of reports announcing her marriage". And hal is an interrogative with the meaning of wishing or of wonder, as a majāz mursal (loose metaphor) by the relation of absolute request, that is: "I wish for that" or "I wonder at its absence".
3- The placing of the prohibition before the command in His words «ألم أعهد إليكم يا بني آدم أن لا تعبدوا الشيطان إنه لكم عدو مبين وأن اعبدوني هذا صراط مستقيم». That is because clearing out (takhliya) has the right to precede adorning (taḥliya), as is established in the science of tawḥīd, and so that His words «هذا صراط مستقيم» are connected to it.

dervis-irab:33-36.t:
* I'rab:
(وَآيَةٌ لَهُمُ الْأَرْضُ الْمَيْتَةُ أَحْيَيْناها): A resumptive speech, delivered to bring a sign of the resurrection and of the oneness of Allah. (آية) is a fronted khabar; (لهم) is an adjective; (الأرض) is a postponed mubtadaʾ; and for the clause (أحييناها) it is permissible to be a ḥāl clause or an adjective; the secret of its being an adjective will come in the section on benefits. (وَأَخْرَجْنا مِنْها حَبًّا فَمِنْهُ يَأْكُلُونَ): Conjoined to (أحييناها); (أخرجنا) is a verb and an agent; (منها) is attached to (أخرجنا); (حبا) is a direct object; the fāʾ is resumptive; and (منه) is attached to (يأكلون).
(وَجَعَلْنا فِيها جَنَّاتٍ مِنْ نَخِيلٍ وَأَعْنابٍ وَفَجَّرْنا فِيها مِنَ الْعُيُونِ): (جعلنا) is a verb and an agent, and the clause is conjoined to (أحييناها); (فيها) is attached to (جعلنا) or to an omitted second direct object of (جعلنا); (جنات) is a direct object; (من نخيل) is an adjective of (جنات); (أعناب) is conjoined to (نخيل); (فجرنا) is likewise a conjunction; (فيها) is attached to (فجرنا); and (من العيون) is an adjective of the omitted object of (فجرنا), that is, "springs being from among the springs". Abū al-Baqāʾ gave its implied form as "what they benefit from, from among the springs", so (من) is partitive. (لِيَأْكُلُوا مِنْ ثَمَرِهِ وَما عَمِلَتْهُ أَيْدِيهِمْ أَفَلا يَشْكُرُونَ): (ليأكلوا) is a reason for what preceded; (من ثمره) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (ليأكلوا); (ما) is a relative or an indefinite noun with a description, conjoined to (من ثمره); the clause (عملته أيديهم) is the ṣila or the description. You may make it a maṣdar, that is, "and from the work of their hands", so it has the meaning of what preceded; as for its i'rab, al-Zamakhsharī said: "You may make (ما) negative, on the basis that the fruit is Allah's creation, not made by the hands of people, and they have no power over it." The hamza is for a question of denial, because nothing is uglier than denying a favour and belittling a kindness; the fāʾ, as has been explained earlier, in a situation like this is a conjunction on an omitted element required by the context, that is, "Do they see these blessings and enjoy them, and then not give thanks for them?"; (لا) is negative; (يشكرون) is an imperfect verb and an agent; and the direct object is omitted, as we indicated.
(سُبْحانَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْأَزْواجَ كُلَّها مِمَّا تُنْبِتُ الْأَرْضُ): (سبحان) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq of an omitted verb, the discussion of which has preceded, and the clause is resumptive, delivered to declare Him, Exalted is He, free of what is unbecoming to Him; (الذي) is a muḍāf ilayhi; the clause (خلق) is the ṣila; (الأزواج) is a direct object; (كلها) is emphasis; (مما) is attached to an omitted ḥāl; and the clause (تنبت الأرض) is the ṣila.
(وَمِنْ أَنْفُسِهِمْ وَمِمَّا لا يَعْلَمُونَ): Conjoined to His saying (مما تنبت الأرض). With this He proceeded through the three matters outside which none of the kinds of created things falls, which are, in order:
1- What the earth grows of grains and kinds of trees.
2- What people beget, male and female.
3- Of pairs of which Allah has not yet informed His servants, and whose reality they have not fathomed.

* Rhetoric:
In His saying «سبحان الذي خلق الأزواج كلها» (the verse) there is the art of correspondence between meanings, or soundness of explanation (ṣiḥḥat al-tafsīr). It is that the speaker brings at the beginning of his speech a meaning whose purport understanding cannot grasp on its own: it is either general and in need of detail, or ambiguous and in need of disambiguation, or open to several readings so that the intended one needs a preference that is only achieved by explaining and clarifying it. The explanation occurs in speech in various ways: sometimes after a condition or after what carries the meaning of a condition, at other times after a preposition and its genitive noun, and at other times after a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the explanation. In this verse, soundness of explanation came joined with soundness of division, and ordering and refinement were folded into both, so that there are four arts in it. He, Glorified is He, put plants first, as we mentioned in the i'rab, and moved, in the way of eloquence, to the higher, so He put second the noblest of animals, which is man, so that mention of him implies the rest of the animals; then He put third His saying:
«ومما لا يعلمون», thus moving from the specific to the general so that it falls under the general. Glory be to Him who sent down the Qur'an.

* Benefits:
Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned that thamar (fruit) is pluralised as thamar with two fatḥas, thamur with two ḍammas, and thumur with ḍamma then sukūn; and no one other than him mentioned more than the first two. [Translator's note: this sentence is translated as written; the forms in the source are unvocalised in the print and the vocalisation given here follows the descriptions in the text.]

dervis-irab:62-67.t:
* Vocabulary:
(جِبِلًّا): with a kasra on the jīm and the bāʾ and a shadda on the lām, like sijill; also jubulan with a ḍamma on the jīm, a sukūn on the bāʾ and a light lām; also jubulan with a ḍamma on the jīm and a sukūn on the bāʾ; also jibilan with a kasra on the jīm and a sukūn on the bāʾ. These are dialectal forms of al-jabal meaning "creation", or a group of it, the least being ten thousand, while the greater has no limit.
(اصْلَوْهَا): taste its heat.
(مَكانَتِهِمْ): al-makāna and al-makān are the same, like al-maqāma and al-maqām; and the meaning is: "We would have transformed them into a transformation that freezes them in their place, unable to leave it".

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ أَضَلَّ مِنْكُمْ جِبِلًّا كَثِيراً أَفَلَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْقِلُونَ): a resumptive clause, brought to intensify the rebuke and confirm the reproach. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath; qad is a particle of certainty; aḍalla is a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent, its implied form being "huwa"; minkum is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to aḍalla; jibillan is the direct object and kathīran an adjective; the hamza is for rhetorical denial (istifhām inkārī), and the fā is a conjunction; lam is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; takūnū is an imperfect defective verb (kāna) jussive by lam, and the wāw is its noun, and the clause taʿqilūna is its khabar (predicate). (هذِهِ جَهَنَّمُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ تُوعَدُونَ): a resumptive clause, brought to confront them with the dreadful destiny to which they will go after the utmost has been reached in rebuking and reproaching them. The demonstrative is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and jahannamu its khabar; allatī is an adjective, and the clause kuntum is a ṣila (relative clause); the tāʾ is the noun of kāna, and the clause tūʿadūna is its khabar.
(اصْلَوْهَا الْيَوْمَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ): iṣlawhā is an imperative verb with its fāʿil and direct object; al-yawma is an adverb attached to iṣlawhā; bi-mā is also attached to iṣlawhā, the bāʾ is causal and mā is a maṣdar particle, that is, "because of your disbelief"; kuntum takfurūna is kāna with its noun and khabar, and the clause kuntum takfurūna has no grammatical position. (الْيَوْمَ نَخْتِمُ عَلى أَفْواهِهِمْ): al-yawma is an adverb of time attached to nakhtimu; nakhtimu is an imperfect verb in the nominative, its fāʿil latent, its implied form being "naḥnu"; ʿalā afwāhihim are also attached to nakhtimu.
(وَتُكَلِّمُنا أَيْدِيهِمْ وَتَشْهَدُ أَرْجُلُهُمْ بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ): wa-tukallimunā aydīhim: an imperfect verb, a fronted direct object and a postponed fāʿil. The secret of the speaking of the hands will come. wa-tashhadu arjuluhum is conjoined to tukallimunā aydīhim; bi-mā are two words attached to tukallimunā, and mā is a maṣdar particle or a relative; kānū is kāna with its noun, and the clause yaksibūna is its khabar.
(وَلَوْ نَشاءُ لَطَمَسْنا عَلى أَعْيُنِهِمْ): the wāw is a conjunction, law is conditional, nashāʾu is an imperfect verb with its fāʿil, and the direct object is omitted, that is, "if We willed their effacement"; the lām occurs in the apodosis of law, and the clause ṭamasnā has no grammatical position; ʿalā aʿyunihim are two words attached to ṭamasnā. al-Ṭams is the splitting of the eye until it becomes effaced; and in al-Miṣbāḥ: "ṭamastu al-shayʾa ṭamsan (of the pattern ḍaraba): I erased it."
(فَاسْتَبَقُوا الصِّراطَ فَأَنَّى يُبْصِرُونَ): the fā is a conjunction, istabaqū is a verb and fāʿil, and the clause is conjoined to laṭamasnā. As for al-ṣirāṭ, al-Zamakhsharī said: "It cannot but be on the omission of the preposition and the verb reaching it directly, the original being fa-istabaqū ilā al-ṣirāṭ; or the verb is made to include the meaning of 'they hastened'; or al-ṣirāṭ is made the thing outstripped rather than the destination of the race; or it is accusative as an adverbial. The meaning is that if He willed, He would have wiped out their eyes, and then, if they wished to race to the well-trodden road they were accustomed to take to their dwellings and to their familiar destinations, which they had frequented often, as they used to race to it, hurrying in their affairs and pressing on in their worldly matters, they would be unable, and it would be too difficult for them to see and know the direction of travel, let alone anything else. Or: if He willed, He would have blinded them, and then, if they wished to walk racing along the familiar road as was their habit, they could not. Or: if He willed, He would have blinded them, and then, if they sought to overtake the path along which they were accustomed to walk, they would be powerless and would not know a road." And al-Samīn said: "al-Ṣirāṭ is a specific adverb of place according to the majority, and therefore they interpreted the verb's reaching it either as its being a direct object figuratively, making it the thing outstripped, and by making istabaqū include the meaning of bādirū, or on the omission of the preposition, that is, ilā al-ṣirāṭ." The fā is a conjunction, and annā is an interrogative noun meaning "how", in the position of accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial); yubṣirūna is an imperfect verb with its fāʿil; the interrogative here has the meaning of negation, that is, "they do not see".
(وَلَوْ نَشاءُ لَمَسَخْناهُمْ عَلى مَكانَتِهِمْ فَمَا اسْتَطاعُوا مُضِيًّا وَلا يَرْجِعُونَ): conjoined to what preceded. law is conditional; nashāʾu is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "naḥnu"; the object of nashāʾu is also omitted, that is, "if We willed their transformation"; the lām occurs in the apodosis of law, and the clause masakhnāhum has no grammatical position; ʿalā makānatihim is a ḥāl, that is, "We would have transformed them in their state", so they would be transformed in their places and in their dwellings. fa-mā: the fā is a conjunction and mā is negative; istaṭāʿū is a verb and fāʿil; muḍiyyan is the direct object; and lā yarjiʿūna is also conjoined, that is, they would not leave their places, and would not be able to flee from them, neither advancing nor retreating.

dervis-irab:37-40.t:
* Vocabulary:
(نَسْلَخُ): "We separate". One says "he skinned (salakha) the sheep's hide" when he stripped it off and removed it, and "he skinned the snake". In the lexicons: salakha yaslakhu, of the pattern naṣara and fataḥa, salkhan: "he skinned the lamb", i.e. stripped off its hide; "the woman took off (salakhat) her tunic", i.e. removed it; and "the snake slipped out (salakhat) of its slough", i.e. it uncovered itself from its slough and its skin, meaning its peel. The word "skinning" was then borrowed for removing light and uncovering it from the place of the night and the spot where its shadow falls.
(العرجون): with ḍamma on the ʿayn; it is also called al-ʿurjud and al-ʿurjudd with shadda on the dāl. It is the base of the date-stalk (ʿidhq) that bends and stays on the palm dry after the clusters (shamārīkh) have been cut from it; the plural is ʿarājīn. Al-Zajjāj said: it is on the pattern fiʿlūn, from inʿirāj, which is bending. The secret of likening the moon to it will come in the section on rhetoric.

* I'rab:
(وَآيَةٌ لَهُمُ اللَّيْلُ نَسْلَخُ مِنْهُ النَّهارَ فَإِذا هُمْ مُظْلِمُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction; (آية) is a fronted khabar; (لهم) is an adjective; (الليل) is a postponed mubtadaʾ; the clause (نسلخ) is a ḥāl clause; (منه) is attached to (نسلخ); (النهار) is a direct object; the fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is the particle of surprise; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ; and (مظلمون) is a khabar. The meaning of (مظلمون) is "entering into darkness". One says "aẓlamnā" just as one says "aʿtamnā", "adjaynā" and "aẓharnā", and likewise "aṣbaḥnā", "aḍḥaynā" and "amsaynā".
(وَالشَّمْسُ تَجْرِي لِمُسْتَقَرٍّ لَها): (الشمس) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (تجري) is the khabar; (لمستقر) is attached to (تجري); the meaning of (المستقر) will be given in the section on benefits; and (لها) is attached to an omitted adjective. (ذلِكَ تَقْدِيرُ الْعَزِيزِ الْعَلِيمِ): (ذلك) is a mubtadaʾ, the pointing being to its running; (تقدير) is its khabar; (العزيز) is a muḍāf ilayhi; and (العليم) is a second adjective. (وَالْقَمَرَ قَدَّرْناهُ مَنازِلَ حَتَّى عادَ كَالْعُرْجُونِ الْقَدِيمِ): The wāw is a conjunction; (القمر) is the direct object of an omitted verb that what follows explains, that is, it is accusative by ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb with a pronoun), and the clause (قدرناه), consisting of the verb, agent and direct object, is explicative. It has also been read with the nominative, on the basis that it is conjoined to the fronted mubtadaʾ, or that it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is (قدرناه). As for (منازل), there are several analyses of it. One is that it is a ḥāl on the omission of a muḍāf, that is, "possessing mansions", because there is no sense in "We determined the moon itself as mansions". The second is that it is a second direct object of (قدرناه), that is, "We made it into mansions". The third is that it is an adverbial, that is, "We determined its course through mansions", and al-Zamakhsharī and al-Jalāl inclined to this analysis. (حتى) is a particle of terminus and of genitive; (عاد) is a past verb whose agent is "huwa" (he), that is, the moon in the last of its mansions. You may make (عاد) defective, in which case the noun is latent and the kāf is a noun meaning "like", the khabar of (عاد); and if you consider it complete, it is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl. (القديم) is an adjective of (العرجون), and the secret of this simile will come in the section on rhetoric.
(لَا الشَّمْسُ يَنْبَغِي لَها أَنْ تُدْرِكَ الْقَمَرَ): (لا) is negative; (الشمس) is a mubtadaʾ; the clause (ينبغي) is the khabar; (لها) is attached to (ينبغي); (أن) and what is in its scope is the agent of (ينبغي); and (القمر) is a direct object. The meaning of the sun's overtaking the moon is the disruption of the determined course and the established order, so that the constitution of the universe and its order not be disturbed. (وَلَا اللَّيْلُ سابِقُ النَّهارِ): Conjoined to what preceded; (الليل) is a mubtadaʾ, (سابق) a khabar, and (النهار) a muḍāf ilayhi. More of its meaning will come. (وَكُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ): (كل) is a mubtadaʾ, and beginning with it is allowed because of the meaning of generality in it and because the tanwīn is a compensation for an omitted annexed word, that is, "each one of the sun, the moon, the stars and the planets"; (في فلك) is attached to (يسبحون); the clause (يسبحون) is the khabar; and the wāw is the agent, because He placed them in the position of those with intellect. The secret of that will come in the section on rhetoric.

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain a good many of the arts of rhetoric:
1- Metaphor (isti'āra):
The first is the implicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya) in His saying «وآية لهم الليل نسلخ منه النهار». He likened the night's severing of itself from the day to the stripping of the hide from the body that is skinned. That is because, when the vanguards (hawādī) of dawn at its rising are fused to the rear of the night, the name "skinning" was applied to them, and that was better than saying "We bring out", for example, because skinning is achieved only with effort and hardship, owing to the extreme adherence of the skin to the flesh and bones [Translator's note: the source reads «إلى بجهد», evidently a misprint for «إلا بجهد» "except with effort"]. The common ground between them is removal and laying bare: just as the sheep is laid bare when its hide is stripped, so the night, when the day is stripped from it, loses its light and its intense blackness appears, flooding the universe with its darkness.
2- Tawshīḥ (anticipation of the rhyme):
In His saying: «وآية لهم الليل نسلخ منه النهار» (the verse) there is the art of tawshīḥ. It is that at the beginning of the speech there is a meaning which, when known, lets the rhyme be known if it is verse, or the saj' (rhymed prose) if it is prose, on condition that the earlier meaning, by its wording, is of the same kind as the meaning of the rhyme or saj' by its wording, or among the necessary implications of its wording. For whoever has memorised the sura and is aware that its verse-endings end with the nūn preceded by a lengthening letter, and hears at the start of the verse the stripping of the day from the night, knows that the verse-ending will be «مظلمون», because one from whom the day has been stripped away becomes dark, that is, enters into darkness for as long as that state lasts.
3- The unrestricted simile (al-tashbīh al-mursal):
That is in His saying «حتى عاد كالعرجون القديم». He likened the crescent to the base of the date-stalk. The ʿidhq, with kasra on the ʿayn, is the kibāsa, and the kibāsa is the cluster of the date palm. It is a wonderful simile for the crescent, for when the ʿurjūn grows old it becomes thin, bent and yellow, and these are the points of resemblance between the crescent and the ʿurjūn: it resembles it to the eye in thinness, not in size, and in curvature and yellowness.
4- Metaphor again:
He borrowed "overtaking" for the sun and "preceding" for the night and the day, to explain what is established in the science of geography of the revolutions of the sun, the moon and the earth and the coming about of night and day. He made the sun one that does not overtake and the moon one that does not precede because the sun is fixed and revolves only in a revolution whose duration is not known, around something entirely unknown to us, and it also has a revolution on its axis, like the earth, which it completes in twenty-five days, or exactly twenty-five days, six hours, sixteen minutes and eight seconds. As for the moon, it has two motions: one around its axis and the second around the earth, each of them proceeding from west to east, and it completes its orbit around the earth in approximately twenty-nine and a half days, and this is what is called the lunar month. So the sun was fit to be described by overtaking because of the slowness of its course, and the moon fit to be described by preceding because of the speed of its course.
5- Preponderance (taghlīb):
He gave preponderance to those with intellect, because He placed the sun, the moon, the stars and the planets in their position. The secret in it is that, since He described them with swimming (sabāḥa), which is among the attributes of those with intellect, that was permissible for Him.

dervis-irab:68-76.t:
* Vocabulary:
(نُعَمِّرْهُ): We prolong his term; ʿammarahu Allāhu (with a shadda) means "Allah made him live long". This root has been mentioned previously in full detail.
(نُنَكِّسْهُ): We reverse him, that is, We make him the opposite of how We created him, so he diminishes until he returns to a state resembling that of a child. In al-Qāmūs and others: "nakkasahu tankīsan (with a shadda) is the same as nakasahu; nakasahu yankusuhu (of the pattern naṣara) nakṣan: he turned it upside down on its head and made its bottom its top and its front its back." And in al-Miṣbāḥ:
"nakastuhu nakṣan (of the pattern qatala): I turned it over, and from it is said walad mankūs when its feet come out before its head, because it is reversed, contrary to the norm; and nukisa al-marīḍ nakṣan, in the passive: the illness returned to the sick person, as if he were turned back to illness." One of them has gathered the meanings of this root and said:
قلب على رأس فهذا نكس ... والرجل الفسل الضعيف نكس رجوع داء بعد برء نكس ... والناكس المرخي لرأس فادر
(Turning over on the head: this is naks; the base, weak man is naks; the return of a disease after recovery is naks; and the nākis is the one who lets his head droop, so know it.)
Among the curiosities of the matter of the nūn with the kāf is that when they occur as the first and second letters of a word, they indicate an effect on a thing accompanied by pain and hurt: naka'a al-qarḥa means he peeled off the sore before it healed, so he made it worse. He said:
ولم تنسني أوفى المصيبات بعده ... ولكنّ نكء القرح بالقرح أوجع
(The greatest of calamities after him did not make me forget him, but the re-opening of a sore upon a sore is more painful.)
And nakaba ʿanhu means he turned away from it; nakaba al-ināʾ means he poured out what was in it; al-nakba is a calamity whose effect is far-reaching, and from it comes al-rīḥ al-nakbāʾ, which is specifically the wind that blows between the east wind and the north wind. Nakata al-arḍa means he struck the ground with his twig or his finger; marra al-faras yankutu means the horse passed, rising from the ground in its running; nakata al-ʿaẓma means he extracted its marrow; fulān nakkāt fī al-aʿrāḍ means he is a slanderer of honours, so what the common people use is close to the correct. Nakatha al-ḥabl (the rope), the siwāk, and the sāʾf at the roots of the nails; intakatha by itself means it came undone and became disordered; and this is nukātha al-ḥabl: what has come undone from its end, and nukātha al-siwāk: what has frayed from its head; and from its figurative use: nakatha al-ʿahd wa-al-bayʿa, to break them, and he is a nakkāth of covenants. Nakaḥa al-marʾata and istankaḥahā: he married the woman. Al-Nābigha said:
وهم قتلوا الطائي بالحجر عنوة ... أبا جابر واستنكحوا أم جابر
(They killed the Ṭāʾī at al-Ḥijr by force, Abū Jābir, and took Umm Jābir in marriage.)
And istankaḥa al-nawmu ʿuyūnahum (sleep took hold of their eyes). ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said: واستنكح النوم الذين تخافهم ... ورمى الكرى بوّابهم فتجدّلا
(Sleep took hold of those you fear, and drowsiness struck their doorkeeper so that he fell prostrate.)
And nakada fulānan ḥājatahu means he withheld it from him or gave him only a little of it; nakada al-ghurāb means the crow was thorough in its stinginess; nakida al-ʿaysh (with a kasra on the kāf) means life became hard and difficult; nakkada ʿayshahu (with a shadda) means he made it nakid; ʿaṭāʾ mankūd and munakkad mean scanty and not wholesome. He said:
وأعط ما أعطيته طيبا ... لا خير في المنكود والناكد
(And give what you give wholeheartedly; there is no good in the stingy and the grudging.)
And nakkada ʿaṭāʾahu bi-al-mann means he spoiled his gift with reproach. Ankara al-shayʾa, nakkarahu and istankarahu: he disliked the thing; it is also said that nakira (with a kasra) is stronger than ankara, and this is strange; and it is said: nakira is with the heart and ankara with the eye. Al-Aʿshā said:
وأنكرتني وما كان الذي نكرت ... من الحوادث إلا الشيب والصلعا
(She did not recognise me, and what she found strange of the events of time was only grey hair and baldness.)
And nakazat al-ḥayya tankuzu means the snake strikes with its nose; nakaza al-baḥr means the sea receded. Nakasha al-biʾr: he drained it or took out the mud in it; so what the common people use is beyond reproach.
And nakaṣa ʿalā ʿaqibayhi is well known (he turned back on his heels), and it is said: fulān ḥaẓẓuhu nāqiṣ, wa-jadduhu nākiṣ (his luck is deficient and his fortune is reversed).
And nakifa minhu (with a kasra on the kāf) and istankafa: he refrained and shrank back out of disdain and pride.
And nakala ʿan al-yamīn wa-ʿan al-ʿaduww nukūlan: he held back from the oath and from the enemy; nakaltuhu ʿan kadhā means I weaned him from such and such; nakkaltu bihi (with a shadda) means I afflicted him with a calamity, or made others refrain from doing what he did; and al-qiʿāb is nakāl (a deterrent punishment). Nakahtuhu means I smelled the odour of his mouth, and nakaha al-shārib fī wajhihi: the drinker breathed in his face, and it is not hidden what effect that produces; and it can come with the sense of goodness, one says he is ṭayyib al-nakha (of good breath), and Abū al-Shamqamaq used it in both senses in his words satirising Dāwūd ibn Bakr, who was governor of al-Ahwāz:
وله لحية تيس ... وله منقار نسر
وله نكهة ليث ... خالطت نكهة صقر
(He has a billy-goat's beard, and a vulture's beak; he has a lion's breath, mixed with a hawk's breath.)
And nakaytu fī al-ʿaduww nikāyatan means I multiplied the wounds upon the enemy; you say: fulān qalīl al-nikāya ṭawīl al-shikāya (he inflicts little harm on the enemy but long in complaint). He said:
قليل النكاية أعداءه ... يراعي الفرار يراخي الأجل
(Little harm does he do to his enemies; he watches for flight and slackens the term.)

* I'rab:
(وَمَنْ نُعَمِّرْهُ نُنَكِّسْهُ فِي الْخَلْقِ أَفَلا يَعْقِلُونَ): a resumptive clause, brought to survey the condition of man, how he changes to weakness after strength and to deficiency after completeness. man is a conditional noun that makes the verb jussive; nuʿammirhu is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), the fāʿil (agent) is latent, its implied form being "naḥnu", and the hāʾ is the direct object; nunakkishu is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "naḥnu", and the hāʾ is the direct object; fī al-khalq are two words attached to nunakkishu or to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial); the hamza is for rhetorical denial, the fā is a conjunction to an omitted clause that the context requires, lā is negative, and yaʿqilūna is an imperfect verb in the nominative with its fāʿil. (وَما عَلَّمْناهُ الشِّعْرَ وَما يَنْبَغِي لَهُ): a resumptive clause, brought to answer those who claimed that the Qur'an is poetry. mā is negative; ʿallamnāhu is a past verb with fāʿil and direct object, and al-shiʿra is a second direct object; wa-mā is a conjunction, and yanbaghī is an imperfect verb conjoined to ʿallamnāhu; lahu are two words attached to yanbaghī. Further clarification on this subject will come.
(إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ وَقُرْآنٌ مُبِينٌ): in is negative, huwa is a mubtadaʾ (subject), illā is a particle of restriction, dhikrun is the khabar (predicate), qurʾānun is conjoined to dhikrun and mubīnun is an adjective. (لِيُنْذِرَ مَنْ كانَ حَيًّا وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ عَلَى الْكافِرِينَ): the lām is causal; yundhira is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied an after the lām, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted element indicated by the context, that is, "it was sent down to him so that he may warn"; man is a direct object, and the clause kāna is a ṣila (relative clause); the noun of kāna is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "huwa", and ḥayyan is its khabar; wa-yaḥiqqa is conjoined to li-yundhira; al-qawlu is the fāʿil, and what is meant by it is the punishment; ʿalā al-kāfirīna are two words attached to yaḥiqqa.
(أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا خَلَقْنا لَهُمْ مِمَّا عَمِلَتْ أَيْدِينا أَنْعاماً فَهُمْ لَها مالِكُونَ): the hamza is for confirmatory interrogation (istifhām taqrīrī). It has been said previously that this construction has two sound aspects. The first is that the original construction is a-wa-lam yaraw, but since the interrogative has the right of the first place, the hamza was put before the wāw. The second is that the sentence is as it stands, and the wāw is a conjunction to an omitted clause that the context requires; we have followed this aspect in most of what we have set out earlier, and the implied form is "a-lam yatafakkarū wa-lam yaraw"; we have repeated it here because of the length of time since. lam is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; yaraw is an imperfect verb jussive by lam, the wāw is the fāʿil, and the seeing is one of knowledge (ruʾya ʿilmiyya); annā and what is within its scope take the place of the two objects of yaraw; anna and its noun, and the clause khalaqnā is its khabar; khalaqnā is a verb and fāʿil; lahum are two words attached to khalaqnā, that is, for their sake and benefit; mimmā are two words attached to an omitted ḥāl; the clause ʿamilat is a ṣila and the returning pronoun is omitted, that is, "ʿamilathu"; aydīnā is the fāʿil, and anʿāman is the direct object of khalaqnā; the fā is a conjunction, hum is a mubtadaʾ, lahā are two words attached to mālikūna, and mālikūna is the khabar of hum; they are such as camels, cattle, sheep, horses and donkeys.
(وَذَلَّلْناها لَهُمْ فَمِنْها رَكُوبُهُمْ وَمِنْها يَأْكُلُونَ): wa-dhallalnāhā is a past verb with fāʿil and direct object, and lahum are two words attached to dhallalnāhā; the fā is for consequence (tafrīʿ), minhā is a fronted khabar and rakūbuhum a postponed mubtadaʾ; wa-minhā are two words attached to yaʾkulūna, and yaʾkulūna is an imperfect verb in the nominative with its fāʿil. (وَلَهُمْ فِيها مَنافِعُ وَمَشارِبُ أَفَلا يَشْكُرُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction, lahum is a fronted khabar, fīhā is a ḥāl, and manāfiʿu is a postponed mubtadaʾ; mashāribu is conjoined to manāfiʿ, and it is the plural of mashrab, a maṣdar mīmī (verbal noun with initial mīm) and a noun of place; the hamza is for rhetorical denial, and the fā is a conjunction as was said before, lā is negative, and yashkurūna is an imperfect verb with its fāʿil. (وَاتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ آلِهَةً لَعَلَّهُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction to an implied clause that the context calls for, that is, "they did not do thankfulness". wa-ittakhadhū is a verb with fāʿil, and min dūni Allāhi is in the place of the second object of ittakhadhū, and ālihatan is its first object; laʿalla and its noun, and the clause yunṣarūna is its khabar, and the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); the clause of hope is a ḥāl, that is, while hoping for help from their gods.
(لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ نَصْرَهُمْ وَهُمْ لَهُمْ جُنْدٌ مُحْضَرُونَ): lā is negative, and yastaṭīʿūna is an imperfect verb with its fāʿil; the pronoun of rational beings is attributed to their gods, treating them as rational beings; naṣrahum is a direct object; the wāw is circumstantial, hum is a mubtadaʾ, lahum is a ḥāl from jundun because it was originally an adjective of it that was fronted; jundun is their khabar, and muḥḍarūna is a second khabar of hum or an adjective of jundun.
(فَلا يَحْزُنْكَ قَوْلُهُمْ إِنَّا نَعْلَمُ ما يُسِرُّونَ وَما يُعْلِنُونَ): the fā is the fā al-faṣīḥa (eloquent fā), that is, if you have known what preceded and are certain that they pin their empty hopes on what deserves loss and calls for the demolition of dreams and the scattering of illusions, then let not their saying grieve you. lā is prohibitive, yaḥzunka is an imperfect verb jussive by the prohibitive lā, the kāf is the direct object, and qawluhum is the fāʿil. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition and said: innā, with a kasra on the hamza; had it been given a fatḥa the meaning would be corrupted. inna and its noun, and the clause naʿlamu is its khabar, the fāʿil being latent, its implied form being "naḥnu"; mā is a direct object, and it is a relative or a maṣdar particle, and the clause yusirrūna has no grammatical position in either case, that is, "that which they conceal" or "their secrets"; wa-mā yuʿlinūna is conjoined to mā yusirrūna, that is, "and that which they declare" or "and their declaring". Al-Zamakhsharī has an enjoyable passage on the kasra of the hamza of inna and its fatḥa, which we cite in the section on benefits.

* Benefits:
Some of those who favour prose and who attack poetry tried to argue that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Exalted in prose, and that the Prophet ﷺ is not a poet because of His words, the Exalted: «وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له»; and he thinks that he has brought the strongest argument. But in fact, when Allah the Exalted sent His Messenger unlettered and not a poet to a people who knew the truth of that from him, at the time when eloquence was in full command and rhetoric well known, it was a sign of prophethood, a proof against creation, and an inimitable challenge to those who practised it; and He made it prose so that it would be a clearer proof of its excellence over poetry, which requires its practitioner to be able to produce what he likes of speech; and He challenged all people, poets and others, to produce the like of it, and that left them powerless. From this Allah the Exalted said «وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له», that is: so that the proof may be established against you, the evidence may be sound in your view, and the demonstration may refute your falsehoods. The meaning: the Qur'an is not poetry, and it is nothing of poetry. How could it be, when poetry is only measured, rhymed speech which indicates a meaning? Where is the metre? Where is the rhyme? Where are the meanings that the poets aim at, compared with its meanings? Where is the composition of any of them compared with its composition and styles?
So there is no relation between it and poetry. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: what of his saying:
أنا النبي لا كذب ... أنا ابن عبد المطلب
(I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.)
and his saying:
هل أنت إلّا إصبع دميت ... وفي سبيل الله ما لقيت
(Are you anything but a finger that bled? And in the path of Allah is what you met with.)
I say: it is nothing but speech of the same kind as his speech which he threw out naturally, without artifice or affectation, except that it happened, without any intention to that or attention from him to it, that it came out metrical, as happens in many of people's compositions in their sermons, letters and conversations: metrical things which no one calls poetry, and which never cross the mind of the speaker or the hearer as poetry; and if you search in every kind of speech for the like of that you will find occurrences in the metres of the seas not rare, besides which al-Khalīl did not count the mashṭūr of rajaz as poetry."
I say: an extensive discussion of poetry has already been given in another place, so renew your acquaintance with it.
Between the kasra of the hamza of inna and its fatḥa:
Al-Zamakhsharī said regarding His words, the Exalted: «فلا يحزنك قولهم إنا نعلم ما يسرون وما يعلنون»: "If you say: what do you say about the one who says: if a reciter recites annā naʿlamu with a fatḥa his prayer is invalidated, and if he believes in what it yields of meaning he disbelieves? I say: there are two aspects to it. One is that it is on the omission of the lām of causation, which is frequent in the Qur'an, in poetry and in all speech, and is a regular analogy; its meaning and the meaning of the kasra are the same. On it is the talbiya of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: inna al-ḥamda wa-al-niʿmata laka; Abū Ḥanīfa gave it a kasra and al-Shāfiʿī a fatḥa, and both are causal. The second is that it is a badal (substitute) of their saying, as if it were said: let not grieve you that We know what they conceal and what they declare; and this meaning also holds with the kasra if you make it the object of the saying.
